blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Confounding handling techniques prevent or remove the distortion of an exposure–outcome association by a confounder (recall §11.6). At the design stage: restriction, matching and randomisation (§15.9). At the analysis stage: stratification, multivariable adjustment and propensity-score methods.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Confounding is a feature of the world, not an error of conduct, so most of it can be handled after data collection, provided the confounder was measured. Which variables count as confounders is decided from a causal diagram (recall §11.6.1), not from the data. The techniques differ in how many confounders they can handle and what they cost.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Does CBHI membership increase use of a health facility? Household wealth affects both joining and facility use. A researcher could restrict the study to one wealth band; match each member to a non-member of similar wealth; stratify by wealth and pool the strata; put wealth in a logistic model beside membership (recall §12.4.1, §13.2.5); or build a propensity score from wealth, education and other confounders (§15.3.1–15.3.2).

points.html: Restriction to a single level of a variable removes confounding by that variable, at the cost of sample size and generalisability. Restriction to a band (such as one wealth band) can leave residual confounding within the band.

Matching in a case-control study makes a matched analysis necessary: the matched-pair OR b/c (recall §10.8) or conditional logistic regression (recall §13.2.9). In the matched EBF case-control study of §10.8, the matched OR was 2.4 and the unmatched OR 2.08. A matched variable’s own effect cannot then be studied.

Stratification with Mantel–Haenszel pooling (recall §11.7) handles one or two confounders; the EBF–diarrhoea RR fell from a crude 3.54 to RR_MH 2.93 after stratifying by PHC. With several confounders the strata multiply and empty out.
Multivariable adjustment handles many confounders at once, if the model’s form is right (recall §12.4.5).
Propensity scores condense many confounders into one number (§15.3.1).
None of these handles an unmeasured confounder. Only randomisation balances unmeasured variables as well as measured ones, on average across possible allocations (§15.9: randomised trials).

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
The propensity score is a subject’s probability of receiving the exposure (being in the exposed group), given measured baseline covariates X:

e(X) = P(E = 1 | X)

It is the same quantity for exposed and unexposed subjects: for a non-member household, it is the probability that a household like it would have joined, not the probability of the (non-)membership it actually has. In Austin’s (2009) words, “the propensity score is a subject’s probability of treatment, conditional on observed baseline covariates.” It is not the probability of the outcome, and it is not an effect estimate.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Multivariable adjustment models the outcome. A propensity score models the exposure instead. Fit a logistic regression with exposure (CBHI membership) as the dependent variable and the confounders as predictors; each household’s fitted probability is its score. The property that makes this useful: “conditional on the true propensity score, treated and untreated subjects have similar distributions of observed baseline covariates” (Austin, 2009). Two households with the same score may differ in wealth and education individually, but among all households with that score, members and non-members have the same distribution of wealth and education. Matching or weighting on one number then balances all the covariates in it.

Which covariates go in: decide from the DAG, before fitting. Recall §11.6.1: adjust for a set that blocks every backdoor path, and never for a descendant of the exposure.

  • Include confounders (causes of both exposure and outcome).
  • Include variables that affect the outcome but not the exposure. In simulations, such variables “should always be included in a PS model. The inclusion of these variables will decrease the variance of an estimated exposure effect without increasing bias” (Brookhart et al., 2006).
  • Avoid variables that affect the exposure but not the outcome (instrument-like variables). “Including variables that are related to the exposure but not to the outcome will increase the variance of the estimated exposure effect without decreasing bias” (Brookhart et al., 2006). An example: which ASHA enrolled the village, if the ASHA affects joining but not facility use by any other route.
  • Exclude mediators and colliders. A mediator lies on the causal path after the exposure, so what matters is when a variable was measured: a variable measured after enrolment, such as a household’s satisfaction with CBHI services, may be a consequence of membership and must be left out. A collider need not come after the exposure: a pre-exposure variable that is a common effect of two unmeasured causes, one of the exposure and one of the outcome, satisfies the classical three-condition test of §11.6, yet adjusting for it opens a non-causal path (this is why §11.6.1 prefers the backdoor criterion).

A logistic regression cannot discover which variables are confounders. It only estimates a probability from the variables a human chose.

Positivity (overlap). For every combination of covariates, both exposure groups must be possible. If every poor household were a non-member, the data could never show what membership does for a poor household, and no statistics could supply it. Check overlap by plotting the scores of both groups before using them. Poor overlap shows up as unmatched subjects, extreme weights, or an answer that describes only a narrow slice of the sample.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
In the CBHI survey, the DAG drawn by the study team treats distance to the facility, the wealth index, maternal education and household size, all recorded as pre-existing household characteristics, as the adjustment set for the question “does membership increase facility use in the past month?”. The propensity model is the logistic regression of membership on these four.

Figure 15.5 (left) shows the scores. Both groups span most of the range: members from 0.09 to 0.77, non-members from 0.04 to 0.79. But the tails are thin. Below about 0.15 there are many non-members and few members; above 0.60 there are 26 members but only 10 non-members. The overlap is adequate in the middle and sparse at the top, which §15.3.2 will pay for. The right panel is a simulated contrast in which one covariate almost fixes exposure: most exposed subjects have scores near 1 and most unexposed near 0, and there is almost no common ground to compare.

blocks.alt: Propensity-score overlap in the CBHI survey and a simulated poor-overlap contrast
blocks.caption: Figure 15.5. Left: propensity scores for CBHI membership (logistic model on distance, wealth, education and household size; 150 members, 350 non-members). Overlap is adequate between about 0.15 and 0.6, but thin above 0.6, where members outnumber non-members 26 to 10. Right: simulated data (illustrative only) with poor overlap, exposure being nearly determined by one covariate.

points.html: Propensity score = P(exposed | measured covariates), for everyone. Not the outcome probability, not an effect, and no help against unmeasured confounding.

Choose covariates from the DAG: include confounders and outcome-only predictors; avoid exposure-only predictors, mediators (anything measured after exposure that it may affect) and colliders (Brookhart et al., 2006).
Check positivity (overlap) before using the scores.

blocks.html: Using Propensity Scores – Matching, Weighting, and Balance

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A propensity score is used in one of three main ways:

  • Matching: pair each exposed subject with an unexposed subject of similar score, commonly within a caliper (a maximum allowed difference); unmatched subjects are dropped.
  • Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPW): keep everyone and give each subject a weight equal to “the inverse of the probability of receiving the treatment that the subject actually received” (Austin, 2011a): 1/e(X) for the exposed, 1/[1 − e(X)] for the unexposed.
  • Stratification: group subjects by quintiles of the score and compare within each group.

Balance is then checked with the standardised mean difference (SMD) of each covariate:

SMD = (x̄_E − x̄_U) ÷ √[(s²_E + s²_U)/2]

and for a binary covariate with proportions p_E and p_U, SMD = (p_E − p_U) ÷ √{[p_E(1 − p_E) + p_U(1 − p_U)]/2} (Austin, 2009).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Matching. Nearest-neighbour matching within a caliper of 0.2 standard deviations of the logit of the score is a common choice; it “minimized the mean squared error of the estimated treatment effect in several scenarios” (Austin, 2011a).

Weighting. The Derivation shows why the weights balance covariates. With these weights the comparison describes the whole sample, the average treatment effect (ATE).

Stratification. Stratifying on quintiles of the score “eliminates approximately 90% of the bias due to measured confounders when estimating a linear treatment effect” (Austin, 2011a, summarising work by Rosenbaum and Rubin that extends a result of Cochran for a single confounder).

Balance, not p-values. The SMD expresses a difference in units of pooled SD, so it can be compared across variables and “is not influenced by sample size” (Austin, 2009). A t-test after matching is influenced by it: matching shrinks the sample, so a covariate that is still imbalanced can give p = 0.6. A common convention treats |SMD| < 0.1 as negligible imbalance; Austin (2009) notes there is “no clear consensus” and that “some researchers have proposed that a standardized difference of 0.1 (10 per cent) denotes meaningful imbalance”.

The estimand. Say which effect, in which population. Matching exposed subjects to controls estimates the average treatment effect in the treated (ATT): “the average effect of treatment on those subjects who ultimately received the treatment” (Austin, 2011a). If some exposed subjects cannot be matched, it is the effect among the matched exposed only. The IPW weights above estimate the ATE.

The outcome analysis is a separate decision. After 1:1 matching, should the analysis respect the pairs? Austin’s simulations favour paired methods: they gave “empirical type I error rates that were closer to the advertised rate” and “narrower 95 per cent confidence intervals” (Austin, 2011b). Stuart (2010) records that “there is debate about whether the analysis needs to account for the matched pair nature of the data” and gives reasons why it may not be necessary. State and justify your choice; a reasonable default for a binary outcome is a paired analysis (McNemar test and matched-pair OR b/c, recall §10.8), with an unpaired analysis as a sensitivity check. After weighting, use a weighted analysis with a robust SE (recall §13.7); after stratification, pool the strata as in §11.7.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Why IPW balances covariates. Take the N_x households in the sample that share covariate values x, with score e = e(x).

  1. About N_x × e of them are members; each gets weight 1/e. Weighted number of members = N_x × e × (1/e) = N_x.
  2. About N_x × (1 − e) are non-members; each gets weight 1/(1 − e). Weighted number = N_x.
  3. So in the weighted data, members and non-members each have N_x households with covariates x, for every x: both groups have the covariate distribution of the whole sample.
  4. The weighted outcome comparison therefore estimates the effect in the whole population (the ATE). When e is close to 0 for a member (or close to 1 for a non-member), the weight explodes: this is the positivity problem in numbers.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Research question: is CBHI membership associated with facility use in the past month, after balancing distance, wealth, maternal education and household size? Crude: 50 of 150 members (33.3%) and 56 of 350 non-members (16.0%) used a facility, a crude risk difference of 17.3 percentage points.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. SMD before matching, distance: members 6.41 km (SD 3.42), non-members 8.12 km (SD 3.03). SMD = (6.41 − 8.12) ÷ √[(3.42² + 3.03²)/2] = −1.71 ÷ √10.46 = −1.71 ÷ 3.23 = −0.53. Wealth: 0.70. Secondary education: 46.0% against 24.6%, SMD = 0.214 ÷ √[(0.46 × 0.54 + 0.246 × 0.754)/2] = 0.214 ÷ 0.466 = 0.46. Large imbalances.
  2. Matching: 1:1 nearest neighbour on the logit of the score, caliper 0.2 SD, without replacement. 133 of 150 members find a partner. The 17 unmatched members all have scores between 0.59 and 0.70: the thin upper tail of Figure 15.5.
  3. Balance after matching: SMDs for distance −0.06, wealth −0.03, secondary education 0.06, no education 0.02, household size 0.04. All below 0.1 in absolute value.
  4. Paired outcome table (133 pairs): both used a facility 8; member only 35; non-member only 16; neither 74. Facility use: members 43/133 = 32.3%, matched non-members 24/133 = 18.0%.
  5. Paired risk difference = (35 − 16)/133 = 0.143. SE = √[35 + 16 − (35 − 16)²/133] ÷ 133 = √48.29 ÷ 133 = 0.0522; 95% CI 0.143 ± 1.96 × 0.0522 = 0.040 to 0.245. Matched-pair OR = 35/16 = 2.19; McNemar χ² = (35 − 16)² ÷ 51 = 7.08, p = 0.008.
  6. Estimand: ATT among the 133 matched members. It does not describe the 17 unmatched members, all from the upper tail of the score (0.59 to 0.70).
  7. IPW (all 500 households): weights range from 1.05 to 11.4; after weighting all SMDs are below 0.03. Weighted facility use: members 27.6%, non-members 15.1%, a difference of 12.5 percentage points (ATE).
  8. Limitation: trust in the formal health system was not measured. If it drives both joining and facility use, none of these estimates removes it.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
cb <- read.csv("data/cbhi_survey.csv")
cb$sec  <- as.integer(cb$maternal_education == "secondary+")
cb$none <- as.integer(cb$maternal_education == "none")
ps_fit <- glm(cbhi_member ~ distance_km + wealth_index +
                maternal_education + household_size,
              family = binomial, data = cb)
# P(member | covariates), for every household
cb$ps <- fitted(ps_fit)
tapply(cb$ps, cb$cbhi_member, range)              # overlap check
smd <- function(x, t) (mean(x[t == 1]) - mean(x[t == 0])) /
  sqrt((var(x[t == 1]) + var(x[t == 0])) / 2)
vars <- c("distance_km", "wealth_index", "sec", "none",
          "household_size")
# 1:1 nearest neighbour on logit(ps), caliper 0.2 SD
lps <- qlogis(cb$ps); cal <- 0.2 * sd(lps)
tr <- which(cb$cbhi_member == 1); tr <- tr[order(-cb$ps[tr])]
pool <- which(cb$cbhi_member == 0); pairs <- NULL
for (i in tr) {
  j <- pool[which.min(abs(lps[pool] - lps[i]))]
  if (abs(lps[j] - lps[i]) <= cal) {
    pairs <- rbind(pairs, c(i, j)); pool <- setdiff(pool, j)
  }
}
nrow(pairs)                                       # members matched
md <- cb[c(pairs), ]
round(rbind(
  before = sapply(vars, function(v) smd(cb[[v]], cb$cbhi_member)),
  after  = sapply(vars, function(v) smd(md[[v]], md$cbhi_member))), 2)
y <- cb$facility_use_past_month
table(member = y[pairs[, 1]], matched_nonmember = y[pairs[, 2]])
tab <- table(y[pairs[, 1]], y[pairs[, 2]])
b <- tab["1", "0"]; c <- tab["0", "1"]; n <- nrow(pairs)
se_rd <- sqrt(b + c - (b - c)^2 / n) / n
rd <- (b - c) / n
round(c(RD = rd, lower = rd - 1.96 * se_rd, upper = rd + 1.96 * se_rd,
        OR_pairs = b / c), 3)
mcnemar.test(tab, correct = FALSE)$p.value
# inverse-probability weighting
library(survey)
cb$w <- ifelse(cb$cbhi_member == 1, 1 / cb$ps, 1 / (1 - cb$ps))
summary(cb$w)
dw <- svydesign(ids = ~village_id, weights = ~w, data = cb)
svyby(~facility_use_past_month, ~cbhi_member, dw, svymean)

The first block is the overlap check (ranges by group). The loop is greedy nearest-neighbour matching, members with the highest scores first; 133 are matched. The SMD table shows balance before and after matching. The 2 × 2 table of pairs gives the paired risk difference, its CI, the matched-pair OR and the McNemar p-value of the Worked Calculation. The last block is IPW: svydesign with the weights and villages as clusters gives weighted facility use by membership with robust SEs. (Dedicated packages exist for matching and balance tables; the base-R version shows every step.)

points.html: Matching, weighting and stratification are three uses of the score; “propensity score” does not mean “matching”.
SMD = difference in means ÷ pooled SD. Convention: |SMD| < 0.1 = negligible imbalance (Austin, 2009; no clear consensus). Check every covariate; do not rely on post-matching p-values.
IPW weight = 1/e for the exposed, 1/(1 − e) for the unexposed → ATE. Extreme weights signal poor overlap.
Matching the exposed → ATT (among the matched). State the estimand.
Paired or unpaired analysis after matching is debated (Austin, 2011b; Stuart, 2010): justify your choice and check the other.

Say “propensity-score methods improve comparability on measured covariates”, never “propensity scores remove confounding”. Doubly robust estimation and sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding (§17.3.1: quantitative bias analysis and the E-value) are beyond this section.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 15.6

questions.prompt: After propensity-score matching, a covariate’s p-value comparing the two groups is 0.62. A colleague concludes that balance was achieved. Why is this premature, and what should be reported instead?
questions.answer: A p-value depends on sample size, and matching usually shrinks the sample, so a covariate that is still clearly imbalanced can give a large p-value. Balance is a property of the sample, not a hypothesis about a population. Report the standardised mean difference for every covariate, before and after matching; a common convention treats |SMD| < 0.1 as negligible (Austin, 2009).

questions.prompt: Before matching, mean age of mothers is 27.0 years (SD 4.0) among members and 25.0 years (SD 5.0) among non-members. Compute the SMD. Is the imbalance negligible by the usual convention?

A team matches 1:1 on the propensity score and reports an odds ratio from ordinary (unpaired) logistic regression on the matched sample. What must the team justify, and what are the two positions in the literature?
questions.answer: They must justify ignoring the pairs. Austin’s (2011b) simulations found that paired methods (for a binary outcome, McNemar’s test and the matched-pair OR b/c, or conditional logistic regression; or robust SEs clustered on the pair) gave type I error and CI coverage closer to nominal. Stuart (2010) records a debate and gives reasons why accounting for the pairs may not be necessary, since matching on the score does not create pairs that are alike on every covariate. The team should state which estimand (ATT among the matched) and which analysis it chose, and report the other as a sensitivity check.
